concept_atlas.summary: A **scalar** has magnitude only (mass, speed, distance, energy, time, temperature). A **vector** has both magnitude and direction (force, velocity, acceleration, weight, displacement, momentum).
formulas: Period T = total time / N oscillations
points: **Measuring Cylinder & Parallax Error:** Read the **bottom of the meniscus** with your eye **perpendicular** to the scale.
**Simple Pendulum:** Time **20 oscillations** from the centre fiducial mark and divide by 20 to reduce human reaction-time error.
**Micrometer Screw Gauge:** Precision `0.01 mm` (main scale + thimble reading minus any zero error).
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Speed and distance are scalars; velocity, displacement, force, weight, and momentum are vectors.

concept_atlas.summary: Motion graphs describe speed, acceleration, and distance travelled using **gradient (slope)** and **area under the graph**.
points: **Distance–Time Graph:** Gradient = **speed**. Horizontal line = at rest (`speed = 0`); straight line sloping up = constant speed; curve getting steeper = acceleration; curve getting flatter = deceleration.

**Speed–Time Graph:** Gradient = **acceleration**; **Area under graph** = **distance travelled**. Horizontal line = constant speed (`a = 0`); straight upward line = uniform acceleration; downward line = uniform deceleration.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: A horizontal line on a **speed–time** graph means **constant speed** (not at rest, unless `speed = 0`).

concept_atlas.topic: Free Fall, Vertical Throw & Terminal Velocity
concept_atlas.summary: Gravity accelerates all objects near Earth downwards at `g ≈ 9.8 m/s²` regardless of mass (when air resistance is negligible).
points: **Ball Thrown Vertically Upwards (at the highest point):** Instantaneous **velocity is `0 m/s`**, but **acceleration is STILL `9.8 m/s²` downwards** because Earth's gravitational force (weight) still acts downwards.

**Terminal Velocity:** Initially `weight > air resistance` so object accelerates downwards. As speed rises, air resistance increases, reducing resultant force and acceleration until **air resistance = weight** (`resultant force = 0`, constant terminal velocity).

**Opening a Parachute:** Surface area increases sharply → air resistance suddenly becomes **greater than weight** → net upward force → object decelerates until a new, lower terminal velocity is reached.

**Why Astronauts Feel Weightless in Orbit:** Gravity STILL acts on them (providing centripetal force), but both the astronaut and spacecraft are in **continuous free fall** together around Earth, so there is zero normal contact force.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Never write 'gravity becomes zero' at the top of a throw or in Earth orbit — gravity still acts!

concept_atlas.summary: **Mass** (`kg`) is the amount of matter (stays constant everywhere). **Weight** (`N`) is the gravitational force on a mass (`W = m × g`). **Density** (`ρ = m / V`) determines whether an object floats or sinks.
formulas: W = m × g  (g ≈ 9.8 N/kg on Earth)
points: **Why a steel ship floats:** The ship is hollow and contains **air spaces**, so its **overall average density** is **less than the density of water**.
**Irregular Solid Density:** Measure mass on a digital balance; measure volume by water displacement in a measuring cylinder or **displacement (Eureka) can**; compute `ρ = m / V`.
**Earth vs Moon:** **Mass stays constant**, whereas **weight decreases** on the Moon because `g` is smaller (`≈ 1.6 N/kg`).
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Mass is measured in `kg` on a balance; weight is a force measured in `N` with a newton-meter.

concept_atlas.topic: Forces, Newton's Laws, Hooke's Law & Circular Motion
concept_atlas.summary: A **resultant force** changes an object's speed, direction (circular motion), or shape (Hooke's law).
points: **Newton's 1st Law (Inertia):** An object stays at rest or continues at **constant velocity** unless acted upon by a non-zero **resultant force**.
**Newton's 2nd Law:** `F = m × a` — resultant force equals mass × acceleration (in the same direction).
**Newton's 3rd Law:** Body A exerts a force on B; B exerts an **equal in magnitude, opposite in direction** force of the **same type** on A.
**Hooke's Law:** Extension (`x`) is directly proportional to load (`F`) up to the **limit of proportionality**.
**Circular Motion:** Even at constant speed, **velocity changes** because **direction changes continuously**, requiring a **resultant centripetal force towards the centre**.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: On an extension–load graph, the **limit of proportionality** is the point where the straight line starts to curve.

concept_atlas.summary: The **moment of a force** measures its turning effect about a pivot: `Moment = Force × perpendicular distance from pivot`.
formulas: Equilibrium: Σ Clockwise moments = Σ Anticlockwise moments
points: **Two Conditions for Equilibrium:** (1) **No resultant force** (`ΣF = 0`), and (2) **No resultant moment** (`ΣM = 0`) about any pivot.
**Stability:** Lower **centre of gravity** and wider **base** give greater stability. An object topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base.
**Irregular Lamina Centre of Gravity:** Hang freely from a pin and draw vertical lines using a **plumb line** from two different holes; their intersection is the centre of gravity.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Always state **perpendicular distance** from the pivot — omitting 'perpendicular' loses the definition mark.

concept_atlas.summary: **Momentum** (`p = m × v`) is conserved in closed systems where no external resultant force acts.
formulas: p = m × v  (kg m/s or N s)
Impulse = F × Δt = Δp = mv − mu
points: **Airbags & Crumple Zones:** Increase the **collision time (`Δt`)** for the same change in momentum (`Δp`), so the **rate of change of momentum (`F = Δp/Δt`) decreases**, reducing the force on the passenger.
**Vector Sign:** Assign `+` to one direction and `−` to the opposite direction during collisions or explosions.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Never say airbags 'reduce momentum' — the momentum change is unchanged; airbags **increase impact time** so **force decreases**.

concept_atlas.summary: Energy is conserved and transferred between stores (**kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear**).
points: **Speed vs Kinetic Energy:** Because `E_k = ½ m v²`, doubling speed increases kinetic energy by **4×** (`2²`).
**Power:** Work done / energy transferred per second (`1 W = 1 J/s`).
**Wasted Energy:** Usually transferred to the surroundings as **thermal (internal) energy** due to friction or air resistance.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Distance `d` in `W = F × d` must be moved **in the direction of the force**.

concept_atlas.summary: **Pressure** is force per unit perpendicular area (`p = F / A`). Liquid pressure increases with depth and density (`Δp = ρ g Δh`).
points: **Small Area vs Large Area:** A sharp knife concentrates force onto a tiny area (`high pressure`); snowshoes spread weight over a large area (`low pressure`).
**Liquid Pressure:** Acts equally in all directions at the same depth and does not depend on container shape.
**Hydraulic Jack:** Liquids are incompressible, so pressure is transmitted equally throughout the fluid; a larger output piston area produces a larger output force.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Convert `cm²` to `m²` by dividing by `10,000` (`1 m² = 10⁴ cm²`) before computing Pascals (`Pa`).

concept_atlas.topic: Kinetic Particle Theory, Brownian Motion & Gas Pressure
concept_atlas.summary: Particles in matter are in continuous random motion; average kinetic energy of molecules increases with **Kelvin temperature**.
points: **Brownian Motion:** Visible smoke/pollen particles move randomly in zig-zag paths because **invisible, fast-moving air/water molecules collide randomly** with them from all directions.

**Gas Pressure:** Gas molecules collide with container walls, changing momentum and exerting a **force per unit area**. Heating a gas makes molecules move **faster** → **more frequent and harder collisions** with the walls → pressure increases.
**Compressing Gas at Constant Temperature (`p₁V₁ = p₂V₂`):** Smaller volume means molecules travel shorter distances between collisions → **more frequent collisions** with walls → higher pressure.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Always mention BOTH **more frequent** collisions AND **greater force / harder** collisions when temperature rises!

concept_atlas.summary: **Evaporation** happens at any temperature below boiling point when the **most energetic molecules escape from the liquid surface**.
formulas: Faster evaporation: higher temperature, larger surface area, air draught/wind, lower humidity
points: **Why Evaporation Causes Cooling:** Only the **fastest (highest kinetic energy) molecules** overcome intermolecular forces and escape from the surface, so the **average kinetic energy** of the remaining molecules decreases → **temperature drops**.

**Evaporation vs Boiling:** Evaporation happens at **any temperature** and **at the surface only** (no bubbles). Boiling happens at a **fixed boiling point** throughout the **entire liquid** (bubbles form).
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: State that **average** kinetic energy of the remaining molecules decreases (not that all molecules stop moving).

concept_atlas.topic: Thermal Expansion, Specific Heat Capacity & Change of State
concept_atlas.summary: **Specific Heat Capacity (`c`)** is the thermal energy needed to raise the temperature of `1 kg` of a substance by `1 °C`. During melting or boiling, temperature stays constant because energy breaks intermolecular bonds.
formulas: E = P × t = V × I × t
points: **Why Temperature Stays Constant During Melting/Boiling:** Supplied thermal energy increases **internal potential energy** to overcome/break **intermolecular forces/bonds**, instead of increasing the average kinetic energy of molecules.
**Thermal Expansion:** Gases expand most, then liquids, then solids (least). Applied in **bimetallic strips** (thermostats, fire alarms) and requires expansion gaps in railway lines and bridges.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Convert mass from **grams to kilograms (`÷ 1000`)** when `c` is in `J/(kg °C)`.

concept_atlas.summary: Thermal energy transfers by **conduction** (mainly solids), **convection** (fluids: liquids & gases), and **infrared radiation** (EM waves — works in a vacuum).
formulas: Convection requires fluid density change; Radiation requires no medium
points: **Conduction (Metals vs Non-Metals):** Atoms vibrate faster and pass kinetic energy to neighbours. Metals conduct far faster because they have **delocalised (free) electrons** that move rapidly through the lattice and collide with ions.

**Why a Metal Spoon Feels Colder Than Wood at Room Temperature:** Both are at the same temperature, but metal is a **good thermal conductor**, so it conducts heat **away from your hand much faster** than wood (an insulator).
**Convection (Fluids Only):** Heated fluid **expands** → its **density decreases** → warmer, less dense fluid **rises** while cooler, denser fluid **sinks**, creating a **convection current**.
**Infrared Radiation:** **Dull, black surfaces** are the **best emitters and absorbers**; **shiny, silver/white surfaces** are **poor emitters/absorbers and good reflectors**.
**Heat Lost vs Heat Gained (Notes p.80):** Heat supplied `<` heat lost → temperature falls; equal → constant; greater → rises.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Convection **never** occurs in solids (particles fixed) or in a vacuum (no particles); **radiation** is the only transfer method through a vacuum.

concept_atlas.topic: Charge, Current, Voltage, Resistance & I–V Graphs
concept_atlas.summary: **Current (`I = Q/t`)** is rate of flow of charge. **Potential difference (`V = E/Q`)** is work done per unit charge. **Ohm's Law** states `I ∝ V` at constant temperature.
points: **Ohmic Resistor `I–V` Graph:** Straight line through origin `(0, 0)` → constant resistance.

**Filament Lamp `I–V` Graph:** As current increases, the filament heats up → metal lattice ions vibrate more vigorously → **more frequent collisions with free electrons** → **resistance increases** and the graph flattens.
**Semiconductor Diode:** Conducts in **one direction only** (forward bias); very high resistance in reverse bias.
**Wire Length & Diameter:** Doubling length `L` doubles resistance; doubling diameter `d` increases area `4×` (`A = πr²`), reducing resistance to **`¼`**.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Connect an **ammeter in series** (very low resistance) and a **voltmeter in parallel** (very high resistance).

concept_atlas.topic: Series & Parallel Circuits, Potential Divider, LDR, Thermistor & Safety
concept_atlas.summary: In **series**, current is identical everywhere and voltages add (`V = V₁ + V₂`). In **parallel**, voltage across each branch equals the supply voltage and currents add (`I = I₁ + I₂`).
formulas: P = I V = I² R = V² / R
E = P t = V I t
points: **Adding a Bulb in Parallel:** Each parallel branch still receives the **full supply voltage**, so existing bulbs keep the **same brightness** (and if one breaks, the others stay on), while total current from the battery increases.
**LDR & NTC Thermistor:** Increasing **light intensity** decreases an **LDR's** resistance; increasing **temperature** decreases a **thermistor's** resistance.

**Fuse & Earth Wire:** The **fuse** is on the **live wire** and melts to break the circuit if current exceeds its rating. The **earth wire** connects metal cases to ground so fault current flows safely to earth and blows the fuse.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: A plastic-cased appliance has **double insulation** and needs no earth wire.

concept_atlas.summary: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a **force** perpendicular to both current and field (**Fleming's Left-Hand Rule**).
formulas: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule: ThuMb = Motion/Force, First finger = Field (N→S), seCond finger = Current (+→−)
points: **Soft Iron vs Steel:** **Soft iron** magnetises and demagnetises easily (electromagnets & transformer cores); **steel** retains magnetism (permanent magnets).

**D.C. Motor & Split-Ring Commutator:** The split-ring commutator **reverses the current direction in the coil every half-turn** (when vertical) so the turning force stays in the **same rotational direction** continuously.
**Increase Motor Turning Effect:** Increase current, use stronger magnets, add more coil turns, or insert a soft-iron core.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Use **Left-Hand Rule** for **Motors** (force from current), and **Right-Hand Rule** for **Generators** (induced current from motion).

concept_atlas.summary: An e.m.f. is induced whenever a conductor **cuts magnetic field lines** (or magnetic flux changes). **Lenz's Law** states the induced current opposes the change causing it.
formulas: Power loss in cables: P_loss = I² × R
points: **A.C. Generator (1st & 2nd Half Cycles — Notes p.148–150):** Uses **slip rings**. Vertical coil → sides move parallel to field → **zero cutting, zero current**. Horizontal coil → cuts field lines at max rate → **maximum current** (reverses direction every half-turn).

**Why Transformers Need a.c. (and Fail With d.c.):** Alternating current creates a **continuously changing magnetic field** in the **soft-iron core** that cuts the secondary coil and induces e.m.f. Direct current creates a **constant magnetic field** (`no cutting` → zero induced voltage).
**High-Voltage Power Transmission:** Step-up transformers raise voltage to **reduce current** (`I = P/V`), drastically cutting thermal power loss **`I²R`** in transmission cables.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Step-up transformers reduce **current** (not resistance) in cables, reducing `I²R` heating loss.

concept_atlas.topic: Nuclear Atom, Alpha/Beta/Gamma, Half-Life, Fission & Fusion
concept_atlas.summary: Radioactive decay is **random and spontaneous**. Unstable nuclei emit **alpha (`⁴₂He`)**, **beta (`⁰₋₁e`)**, or **gamma (`γ`)** radiation.
points: **Rutherford Gold Foil Experiment:** Most α-particles passed straight through (**atom is mostly empty space**); a few deflected/bounced back (**tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus**).
**Penetration & Ionisation:** α is **most ionising** (stopped by paper/skin); β is moderate (stopped by `~3 mm` aluminium); γ is **most penetrating** (reduced by thick lead/concrete).
**Half-Life (`t_½`):** Average time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (always subtract **background radiation** first!).
**Fission vs Fusion:** **Fission** splits a heavy nucleus (`U-235`) using a neutron; **Fusion** joins two light nuclei (hydrogen → helium) at extreme temperature & pressure (powers the Sun & stars).
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Subtract **background count rate** BEFORE calculating half-life, and add it back if asked for a detector reading.

concept_atlas.topic: Wave Properties, Diffraction, Sound & EM Spectrum
concept_atlas.summary: Waves transfer **energy without transferring matter**. Wave speed `v = f × λ`.
points: **Transverse vs Longitudinal:** Transverse vibrates **perpendicular** to wave direction (light, water, all EM waves); Longitudinal vibrates **parallel** via compressions & rarefactions (sound).
**Diffraction:** Waves spread out through a gap/around an edge. **Greatest diffraction** when **gap width ≈ wavelength (`λ`)**. Wavelength, frequency, and speed stay **unchanged**.
**Deep → Shallow Water (Ripple Tank):** Speed **decreases**, wavelength **decreases**, **frequency stays constant**, wavefronts bend **towards normal**.

**Sound Pitch & Loudness:** Higher **frequency** → higher **pitch**; larger **amplitude** → **louder** sound. Sound travels fastest in **solids**, slowest in **gases**, and cannot travel in a **vacuum**.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: During refraction or change of water depth, **frequency NEVER changes** (only speed and wavelength change).

concept_atlas.topic: Reflection, Refraction, Critical Angle, TIR & Lenses
concept_atlas.summary: Light obeys reflection (`i = r`), refraction (`n = sin i / sin r`), and **Total Internal Reflection** (`i > c` from dense to less dense medium).
formulas: n = sin i / sin r = c_air / v_medium
points: **Total Internal Reflection (TIR):** Occurs ONLY when (1) light travels from **optically denser to less dense medium** (e.g. glass → air), AND (2) **angle of incidence > critical angle (`i > c`)**.
**Optical Fibres:** Light travels inside a high-index glass core reflecting repeatedly by **TIR** — used in high-speed internet and medical **endoscopes**.
**Converging Lens (`f`):** `u > 2f` → real, inverted, diminished; `f < u < 2f` → real, inverted, magnified; **`u < f`** → **virtual, upright, magnified** (magnifying glass).
**Dispersion:** White light splits in a prism because **violet** travels slowest in glass and refracts **most**, while **red** refracts **least**.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Measure angles `i` and `r` from the **normal** (perpendicular to the surface), never from the glass surface.

concept_atlas.topic: Solar System, Orbital Speed, Stellar Life Cycle, Redshift & Big Bang
concept_atlas.summary: Gravity provides the centripetal force keeping planets, moons, and comets in orbit. Redshift and CMBR provide evidence for the **expanding Universe** and **Big Bang**.
points: **Comet Orbits:** Elliptical orbit; comet moves **fastest when closest to the Sun** (GPE transfers to KE as gravitational attraction is strongest).

**Life Cycle of Stars:** Nebula → Protostar → Main Sequence (stable: inward gravity = outward radiation pressure). **Sun-like star:** Red Giant → Planetary Nebula + **White Dwarf**. **Massive star:** Red Supergiant → **Supernova** → **Neutron Star** or **Black Hole**.
**Redshift & Big Bang:** Light from distant galaxies shows an **increase in observed wavelength**, proving galaxies are receding — **further galaxies move faster** (`v = H₀ d`).
**CMBR:** Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation fills all of space uniformly — cooled leftover thermal radiation from the hot early Universe.
concept_atlas.examiner_trap: Say redshift is an **increase in observed wavelength** (not 'the galaxy turns red').

When a driver encounters an obstacle, he takes actions to stop the car.
It only takes the driver a brief moment to realize the presence of the obstacle and decide to
apply the brakes, which involves swiftly shifting his foot from the accelerator pedal to the
brake pedal.
This brief interval is commonly referred to as the reaction time. Throughout this
duration, the car continues to move at its regular and constant speed.
The distance covered by the car during this short timeframe is referred to as the
thinking distance, and it can be calculated using the equation v = d/t, where:
"d" represents the thinking distance.
"v" represents the car's speed.
"t" represents the reaction time.
As the driver applies the brakes, the car requires a certain amount of time to come to a
complete stop, during which it undergoes deceleration. In this brief interval, the car travels a
distance known as the braking distance.

Kinetic Theory
1. All matter is built up of small particles (molecules).
2. Molecules are in continuous motion as they have kinetic energy,
3. There are intermolecular attraction forces between molecules.
4. There are intermolecular spaces separating molecules.

Smoke particles are seen as bright specks against dark
background moving in random directions.

and slow are being hit by air molecules
which are small, light, fast and invisible
under a normal microscope, randomly from all directions.

move short distances in zigzag pathway this is
Brownian motion.

molecules will be more energetic and faster.

• Pollen grains in water,
• Ink in water,
• Brownian motion proves that matter is made up of particles and these particles are in
continuous motion.
• When a load extends a spring intermolecular spaces
increases, but intermolecular forces pull molecules back
together when load is removed.
• When a spring is compressed intermolecular spaces
decreases, but intermolecular forces push molecules back
together when compression is removed.
• The elasticity of a spring proves the presence of forces
between molecules and atoms.

have another way that improves conduction,

•
Every substance whether it is a solid, liquid or gas, has a specific heat capacity.

Knowing the value of the specific heat capacity can tell you if this substance will
heat up quickly or slowly.
•
A substance with a small value of specific heat capacity will heat up quickly if
heated with any source of heat.
•
A substance with a larger value of specific heat capacity will heat up slowly if
heated with the same source of heat.
•
All metals are good conductors because they heat up and cool down quickly and they
have small values of the specific heat capacity.
•
All bad conductors of heat up and cool down slowly because they have large value of
the specific heat capacities.
•
A material that heats up quickly can also cool down quickly.

the Sun which is our star, and all the objects which orbit it. It includes the following:

Gravity pulled dust and gas together so they joined to make rocks which then join to make
larger rocks.

it led to the formation of the inner, rocky planets.

The intense heat forced some of the lighter materials further away and these formed the
outer planets - the gas giants.

The four inner planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars,

are small and rocky. After Mars there is the asteroid belt. This is made up of left-over

Solar System
•
Although the planets are small compared to the Sun, they are very massive objects.
•
The more massive the planet, the greater the gravitational force experienced by objects at
its surface.
•
On Earth we experience a force of l0 N/kg.
•
On Earth a 60 kg student has a weight of 600 N.
•
On Mercury, where gravity is 4 N/kg, the same student would weigh 240 N.
•
The gravitational pull of planets is enough to cause moons to orbit them.
•
The orbits of the planets are not
completely circular.
•
The orbits are described as
elliptical.
•
The amount the orbit is squashed is
called its eccentricity.
•
Comets have very eccentric orbits.
•
Comets travel far from the Sun
and then return close to it.
Why are orbits elliptical?
•
Imagine an object moving past the Sun at high speed.
•
As it passes near the Sun the gravitational force of the Sun starts to act on the
object and to pull it towards the Sun.
•
This force also causes it to accelerate.
•
This means the mass speeds up and its kinetic energy carries it slightly further out to the
furthest point of the orbit.
•
The object slows down and is pulled in again towards the Sun.
•
The Sun is not quite at the centre of a planet's elliptical orbit.
•
There is a point close to the centre of an ellipse called the focus.
•
The Sun is at the focus of the elliptical path of each of the planets.
•
The planet moves closer to, and further away, from the Sun during each orbit.
•
The Sun's gravity pulls the object in, speeds it up and then the speed carries it on to the
furthest part of the orbit.
•
The object's orbital speed is therefore greatest when it is nearest to the Sun and slowest
when it is furthest from the Sun.
•
Comets, which have the most elliptical orbits of any body in the Solar System accelerate
greatly as they approach the Sun and are slung back at high speed to the far reaches of
their orbits.
•
A planet orbiting in space does not experience any friction or air resistance, so its energy
remains the same throughout its orbit. It has two types of energy:
•
kinetic energy
•
gravitational potential energy.

The Sun is an average or medium mass star

and is made up of about 75% hydrogen

Stars are powered by nuclear reactions that release energy.

Stable stars like our Sun are powered by the nuclear fusion (or thermonuclear fusion) of
hydrogen into helium.
•
This makes the Sun shine. It is so hot inside the Sun that matter exists as plasma (positive

•
This is the zone where water can exist
in liquid form (an essential requirement
for life as we know it).
•
If it was hotter, the water vapour would never condense; if it was colder, ice would never
melt.
•
The Sun has a mass of 2 x 1030 kg.
•
This is referred to as the solar mass as it provides a simple way of comparing the
mass of other stars to the mass of our Sun.
•
For example, a star with eight solar masses would have eight times the mass of the Sun.

The Sun contains over 98.86% of the mass of the Solar System so it exerts a big
gravitational force on the planets and causes them to follow nearly circular orbits.

A protostar is the first step in star formation.
•
Stars form from interstellar clouds of gas and dust that contain hydrogen called
molecular clouds, which are both cold and dense enough for star formation.
•
The collapse of a clump of molecular cloud due to gravitational attraction starts a
series of energy transfers.
•
As the force of gravity pulls the hydrogen gas molecules closer together, their
gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy.
•
As the molecules collide, their kinetic energy is transferred into thermal energy.
•
The clump contracts into a spinning sphere of super-hot gas known as a protostar.
•
A protostar continues to grow by pulling in more material from the molecular cloud.
•
Its final mass determines what happens to it.
•
A protostar becomes stable when the inward force of gravitational attraction is
balanced by an outward force due to the high temperature of a star caused by
nuclear fusion.

from its parent molecular cloud

An increase in the core temperature of a star increases the radiation pressure and the

A star shrinks when its core temperature falls.

In 1814, Joseph Fraunhofer noticed that many dark lines cross the spectrum of sunlight.
•
These dark lines are the wavelengths of light missing from the sunlight because the cool gas in
the Sun's atmosphere absorbs them.
•
A spectrum with these absorption lines
is known as an absorption
spectrum.
•
These lines allow astronomers to work

•
The spectrum for hydrogen and other elements has been found in experiments on Earth.
•
However, when astronomers looked for the same spectra in distant galaxies, they discovered
that they are redshifted (shifted towards the red end of the spectrum).
•
It means light shifts towards longer wavelengths because the wave is stretched out and the
wavelength is increased.
•
For example, as can be seen in Figure 25.11, absorption lines that are normally in the blue part
of the spectrum can shift into the green part of the spectrum.

• As a very fast vehicle passes you,
the volume of the sound rises and
falls.
• However, the pitch also increases as
the vehicle approaches and decreases
as it recedes (moves away).
• The sound wave is compressed in front of the vehicle as it approaches.
• The sound wave is stretched out behind the vehicle as it moves away.
• Figure: This diagram shows wavefront of a sound wave modified by the Doppler effect, with
the wave compressed ahead of the ambulance (so person A hears a higher pitch) and
redshifted behind (so person B hears a lower pitch).
• The Doppler effect is a property of all waves, including light.
• Light from galaxies that are moving away from us is redshifted.
• This turned out to be the first important clue that the Universe is expanding and suggested
that the galaxies must have been closer together in the past.
• This led to the theory that the Universe had a beginning: the Big Bang theory.
• This is the idea that the Universe (space, time, matter, energy) was created at a single point
13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding and cooling ever since.
• He wants to work out how fast galaxies are moving away from us (or towards us).

and the recession speed of the galaxy (speed of going away from us.

1. Distance of galaxy from us.
2. Speed of galaxy moving away from us (recession speed).
• The speed of the galaxies is directly proportional to the amount of redshift.
• So by studying the light coming from a galaxy we can know its speed from the amount of
redshift that happened to light.

5
Stars and galaxies
cosmic microwave background radiation
• In 1964, the US scientists Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson built a radio telescope but
struggled to eliminate noise (unwanted signal).
• It did not matter where in the sky they pointed their telescope, the noise was constant, and so
they assumed that it was a problem with their equipment.
• However, it turned out that they had accidentally discovered microwave radiation.
• Our best knowledge at the moment is that the Universe began as a hot big bang from a tiny
point smaller than a pinhead (called a singularity) about 13.8 billion years ago.
• The Universe was unimaginably hot and dense but it has been expanding and cooling ever since.
• The early Universe was so hot that neutral atoms could not form. They would instantly ionize.
• Light was continuously scattered off the charged particles (ions and electrons).
• By analogy, light is scattered in fog, which is why you cannot see very far into it.
• Once the Universe was about 379 000 years old, and about the size of the Milky Way, the
temperature dropped to 3000 K and neutral atoms formed.
• Light was no longer scattered and the Universe became transparent.
• It was like the fog suddenly lifted (disappeared) and the air became clear.
• However, the continued expansion of the Universe has caused the wavelength of this light to
redshift over time.

the slope of a graph of galaxy speed against distance
Hubble’s time:
the inverse of the Hubble constant,
which gives an estimate for the age of the Universe

Stars and galaxies
• The wavelength of this light, in the microwave region of the electromagnetic spectrum, was
predicted in 1948.
• They were looking at light that had left the surface of last scattering when the universe was
only 379000 years old (almost 14 billion years ago) and had been redshifted so that its
wavelength was now more than 1000 times longer.
• This microwave radiation, called cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR).
• Penzias and Wilson were awarded the Nobel Prize for physics in 1978 for their accidental
discovery.
• Despite the name, the Big Bang was not an explosion.
• It is the expansion of the space between the galaxies.
• Imagine your universe is the two-dimensional surface of a balloon.
• Everything inside or outside of the balloon does not exist.
• As space expands (that is, the balloon inflates), clusters of galaxies move further apart with
their recession speeds increasing with distance.
• No matter the direction we look, galaxies appear to be moving away from us, suggesting we
are at the centre of the Universe.
• Actually, the Universe does not have a centre or an edge. Do not worry if you (find this idea
impossible to imagine because nobody can.
• The best we can do is to present models.
• Supernovae occur when a large star explodes.
• The important point is that these supernovae always have the same luminosity (output power)
therefore they act as a 'standard candle'.
• By recording how bright the supernova appears to be and knowing how bright it really is, it is
possible to work out how far away it is.
• Scientists are still not able to explain why the expansion of the Universe is speeding up, but
they have suggested that something called 'dark energy' is responsible.

Cambridge IGCSE Physics (0625) Calculation & Marking Rules (Harony Physics Clinic):
1. Always state the formula in symbols or words first (earns C1 / M1 method mark even if arithmetic slips).
2. Convert all quantities to SI base units before substituting: km -> ×1000 m, cm -> ÷100 m, mm -> ÷1000 m, g -> ÷1000 kg, min -> ×60 s, kJ -> ×1000 J, kW -> ×1000 W, mA -> ÷1000 A, kΩ -> ×1000 Ω, kPa -> ×1000 Pa.
3. Give final numerical answers to 2 or 3 sign if i cant figures with the correct SI unit.

chunks.topic: The Universe, Redshift, Hubble's Law & Orbital Speed
chunks.text:
Space Physics Key Equations & Concepts (Cambridge IGCSE 0625 Unit 7):
• Average orbital speed: v = 2πr / T, where r is average orbital radius and T is orbital period.
• Hubble's Law: H₀ = v / d, where v is recession speed of galaxy, d is distance, and H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹.
• Age of the Universe estimate: t = 1 / H₀ = d / v ≈ 13.8 billion years (4.5 × 10¹⁷ s).
• 1 light-year = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m (distance travelled by light in a vacuum in one year).
• Redshift & Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) provide key evidence for the Big Bang theory.
